title: The forest monks
hook: the Thai forest tradition: monks in the jungle, keeping the old rules closely

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tipitaka, and your line, a book made of marble. Today, monks who went back to the trees.

So much of the Buddha's life happened under trees. He was born, the story goes, in a grove, his mother holding a branch. He woke up under a tree. He gave his first teaching in a deer park. He died lying between two trees in a forest. The early monks lived in forests, slept at the roots of trees, and walked into villages only to collect food. Over the centuries many monasteries moved into towns and cities, and that's natural. But about a hundred years ago, in the northeast of Thailand, a handful of monks walked back into the jungle.
screen: `BORN IN A GROVE.` → `AWAKE UNDER A TREE.` → `BACK INTO THE JUNGLE.`

segments.voice: The best-known was Ajahn Mun, born in 1870 in Isan, the region of Thailand near the Lao border. Ajahn means teacher. With his own teacher, Ajahn Sao, he chose a hard life: wandering on foot through the forests of Thailand and Laos, sleeping under a cloth tent hung with a mosquito net, meditating through the night, and keeping the monastic rules as closely as the old texts describe. The forests then were full of tigers, snakes and malaria. The practice has an old name, dhutanga, a set of voluntary austerities listed in the commentaries: eating one meal a day, eating only from the bowl, living at the foot of a tree. Monks who took up the wandering life were called thudong monks, from that word. Ajahn Mun trained a generation of students. One of them, Ajahn Chah, founded a forest monastery in 1954 near the city of Ubon, and later a monastery for foreign monks. Through his students, forest monasteries now stand in England, Australia, New Zealand, the United States and beyond, where monks still walk for alms in the morning. Ajahn Chah liked to compare a trained mind to a still forest pool, where all kinds of wild animals come to drink, and you can watch them clearly. Most of the forests Ajahn Mun walked through have since been cut down. The monasteries became islands of trees. And the tradition keeps a simple conviction: the Buddha's teaching began in the forest, and the forest remembers.
screen: `AJAHN MUN WALKS INTO THE FOREST.` · `DHUTANGA: THE OLD AUSTERITIES.` · `AJAHN CHAH AND THE STILL POOL.` · `MONASTERIES AS ISLANDS OF TREES.` · then, large: `THE FOREST REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Picture a forest monastery: a clearing among tall trees, a simple wooden hall open on the sides, a swept path where a monk walks slowly back and forth, cicadas, a distant bird, cool early air. Then let the picture fade and imagine your mind as a still forest pool. Thoughts come to drink like animals at the edge; you don't chase them, you watch.
Arañña. The forest: where the Thai forest monks, following Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Chah, kept the old rules closely, deep among the trees.
Your line: the forest remembers. Watch the pool; don't chase what comes to drink. Day two hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: In Thai forest monasteries in Thailand and abroad, monks eat one meal a day from the alms bowl, practice walking and sitting meditation, and keep the monastic rules strictly; lay visitors often come to stay and practice.

walk into the forest, keeping the old rules closely.

original.note: Pali arañña: forest, wilderness; a forest monk is an araññavāsī, a forest dweller.

trapdoor: what you thought: forest monks are hermits who reject other Buddhists.
what it means: a revival of the early forest life inside Thai Buddhism, keeping the old rules closely, now worldwide.
what a scholar hears: the thirteen dhutangas are listed in Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga, and scholars note that the forest movement grew as Thailand's forests were being cleared.
recall: a Chan master known for very short answers

chat.says: Why did some Thai monks go back to living in the forest?
options: To live as the early monks did, keeping the old rules closely among the trees.
Because towns stopped letting monks collect food in the mornings.
Because they believed the cities had no monks left to teach them.
chat.meaning: Ajahn Mun and his students chose the early monks' wandering forest life, keeping the monastic rules as closely as the old texts describe.
